Here \(y=\sqrt{x}\), \(x>0\). Writing \(x\) as a function of \(y\), the inverse function is
\(x=y^{2}\), where \(y>0\).
Differentiating \(x\) with respect to \(y\),
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=2y\).
Since \(\frac{dx}{dy}=2y\neq 0\) for \(y>0\), the derivative of the original function is its reciprocal:
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)}=\frac{1}{2y}\).
Putting back \(y=\sqrt{x}\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\), for \(x>0\).

Here \(y=\sqrt{2-\sqrt{x}}\), so \(y\geq 0\).
Squaring, \(y^{2}=2-\sqrt{x}\), hence \(\sqrt{x}=2-y^{2}\) and the inverse function is
\(x=\left(2-y^{2}\right)^{2}\).
Differentiating \(x\) with respect to \(y\),
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=2\left(2-y^{2}\right)\cdot(-2y)=-4y\left(2-y^{2}\right)\).
Therefore
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)}=\frac{-1}{4y\left(2-y^{2}\right)}\).
Now \(y=\sqrt{2-\sqrt{x}}\) and \(2-y^{2}=\sqrt{x}\), so
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-1}{4\sqrt{x}\,\sqrt{2-\sqrt{x}}}\), for \(0<x<4\).

Here \(y=\sqrt[3]{x-2}=(x-2)^{\frac{1}{3}}\).
Cubing, \(y^{3}=x-2\), so the inverse function is
\(x=y^{3}+2\).
Differentiating \(x\) with respect to \(y\),
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=3y^{2}\).
Since \(\frac{dx}{dy}\neq 0\) for \(y\neq 0\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)}=\frac{1}{3y^{2}}\).
Putting back \(y=(x-2)^{\frac{1}{3}}\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{3(x-2)^{\frac{2}{3}}}\), for \(x\neq 2\).

Here \(y=\log(2x-1)\), \(x>\frac{1}{2}\).
Taking exponentials, \(2x-1=e^{y}\), so the inverse function is
\(x=\frac{e^{y}+1}{2}\).
Differentiating \(x\) with respect to \(y\),
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{e^{y}}{2}\).
Since \(\frac{dx}{dy}\neq 0\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)}=\frac{2}{e^{y}}\).
Putting back \(e^{y}=2x-1\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{2x-1}\), for \(x>\frac{1}{2}\).

Here \(y=2x+3\).
Solving for \(x\), the inverse function is
\(x=\frac{y-3}{2}\).
Differentiating \(x\) with respect to \(y\),
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{2}\).
Since \(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{2}\neq 0\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)}=2\).

Here \(y=e^{x}-3\), so \(e^{x}=y+3\) and \(y>-3\).
Hence the inverse function is
\(x=\log(y+3)\).
Differentiating \(x\) with respect to \(y\),
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{y+3}\).
Since \(\frac{dx}{dy}\neq 0\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)}=y+3\).
Putting back \(y+3=e^{x}\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x}\).

Here \(y=e^{2x-3}\), so \(y>0\).
Taking logarithms, \(2x-3=\log y\), hence the inverse function is
\(x=\frac{\log y+3}{2}\).
Differentiating \(x\) with respect to \(y\),
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{2y}\).
Since \(\frac{dx}{dy}\neq 0\) for \(y>0\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)}=2y\).
Putting back \(y=e^{2x-3}\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=2e^{2x-3}\).

Here \(y=\log_{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\), \(x>0\).
By the definition of a base-\(2\) logarithm, \(\frac{x}{2}=2^{y}\), so the inverse function is
\(x=2^{y+1}\).
Differentiating \(x\) with respect to \(y\),
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=2^{y+1}\log 2\).
Since \(\frac{dx}{dy}\neq 0\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)}=\frac{1}{2^{y+1}\log 2}\).
Putting back \(2^{y+1}=x\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{x\log 2}\), for \(x>0\).

Here \(y=x^{2}\cdot e^{x}\). The derivative of the inverse function is \(\frac{dx}{dy}\), the reciprocal of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).
Differentiating \(y\) with respect to \(x\) by the product rule,
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=2x\cdot e^{x}+x^{2}\cdot e^{x}=x\,e^{x}(2+x)\).
Hence, wherever \(\frac{dy}{dx}\neq 0\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}=\frac{1}{x\,e^{x}(x+2)}\), provided \(x\neq 0\) and \(x\neq -2\).

Here \(y=x\cos x\). The derivative of the inverse function is \(\frac{dx}{dy}\).
Differentiating \(y\) with respect to \(x\) by the product rule,
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=1\cdot\cos x+x\cdot(-\sin x)=\cos x-x\sin x\).
Hence, wherever \(\frac{dy}{dx}\neq 0\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}=\frac{1}{\cos x-x\sin x}\), provided \(\cos x-x\sin x\neq 0\).

Here \(y=x\cdot 7^{x}\). The derivative of the inverse function is \(\frac{dx}{dy}\).
Differentiating \(y\) with respect to \(x\) by the product rule, and using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(7^{x}\right)=7^{x}\log 7\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=1\cdot 7^{x}+x\cdot 7^{x}\log 7=7^{x}\left(1+x\log 7\right)\).
Since \(7^{x}\neq 0\) always,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}=\frac{1}{7^{x}\left(1+x\log 7\right)}\), provided \(1+x\log 7\neq 0\).

Here \(y=x^{2}+\log x\), \(x>0\). The derivative of the inverse function is \(\frac{dx}{dy}\).
Differentiating \(y\) with respect to \(x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=2x+\frac{1}{x}=\frac{2x^{2}+1}{x}\).
Since \(2x^{2}+1>0\), we have \(\frac{dy}{dx}\neq 0\) for \(x>0\). Hence
\(\therefore\ \frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}=\frac{x}{2x^{2}+1}\), for \(x>0\).

Here \(y=x\log x\), \(x>0\). The derivative of the inverse function is \(\frac{dx}{dy}\).
Differentiating \(y\) with respect to \(x\) by the product rule,
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=1\cdot\log x+x\cdot\frac{1}{x}=\log x+1\).
Hence, wherever \(\frac{dy}{dx}\neq 0\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}=\frac{1}{1+\log x}\), for \(x>0\), \(x\neq\frac{1}{e}\).

Here \(y=x^{5}+2x^{3}+3x\).
Differentiating with respect to \(x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=5x^{4}+6x^{2}+3\).
Since \(5x^{4}+6x^{2}+3>0\) for every real \(x\), \(\frac{dy}{dx}\neq 0\) and the inverse function is differentiable, with
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}=\frac{1}{5x^{4}+6x^{2}+3}\).
At \(x=1\): the corresponding value of \(y\) is \(y=1+2+3=6\), and
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{5(1)^{4}+6(1)^{2}+3}=\frac{1}{5+6+3}\).
\(\therefore\ \left.\frac{dx}{dy}\right|_{x=1}=\frac{1}{14}\), i.e. \(\left(f^{-1}\right)'(6)=\frac{1}{14}\).

Here \(y=e^{x}+3x+2\).
Differentiating with respect to \(x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x}+3\).
Since \(e^{x}>0\), \(\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x}+3>0\) for every real \(x\), so the inverse function is differentiable, with
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}=\frac{1}{e^{x}+3}\).
At \(x=0\): the corresponding value of \(y\) is \(y=e^{0}+0+2=3\), and
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{e^{0}+3}=\frac{1}{1+3}\).
\(\therefore\ \left.\frac{dx}{dy}\right|_{x=0}=\frac{1}{4}\), i.e. \(\left(f^{-1}\right)'(3)=\frac{1}{4}\).

Here \(y=3x^{2}+2\log x^{3}\), \(x>0\).
Using \(\log x^{3}=3\log x\), we get \(y=3x^{2}+6\log x\).
Differentiating with respect to \(x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=6x+\frac{6}{x}=\frac{6\left(x^{2}+1\right)}{x}\).
This is non-zero for \(x>0\), so
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}=\frac{x}{6\left(x^{2}+1\right)}\).
At \(x=1\): the corresponding value of \(y\) is \(y=3+6\log 1=3\), and
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{6(1+1)}\).
\(\therefore\ \left.\frac{dx}{dy}\right|_{x=1}=\frac{1}{12}\), i.e. \(\left(f^{-1}\right)'(3)=\frac{1}{12}\).

Here \(y=\sin(x-2)+x^{2}\).
Differentiating with respect to \(x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\cos(x-2)+2x\).
Hence, wherever this is non-zero,
\(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}=\frac{1}{\cos(x-2)+2x}\).
At \(x=2\): the corresponding value of \(y\) is \(y=\sin 0+4=4\), and
\(\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=2}=\cos 0+2(2)=1+4=5\neq 0\).
\(\therefore\ \left.\frac{dx}{dy}\right|_{x=2}=\frac{1}{5}\), i.e. \(\left(f^{-1}\right)'(4)=\frac{1}{5}\).

Here \(f(x)=x^{3}+x-2\). We use \(\left(f^{-1}\right)'(y)=\frac{1}{f'(x)}\), where \(y=f(x)\).
Since we want \(\left(f^{-1}\right)'(0)\), we first find the \(x\) for which \(f(x)=0\).
\(x^{3}+x-2=0\)
\(\Rightarrow (x-1)\left(x^{2}+x+2\right)=0\).
The quadratic factor \(x^{2}+x+2\) has discriminant \(1-8=-7<0\), so it has no real zero. Hence \(x=1\) is the only real solution, i.e. \(f(1)=0\).
Now differentiate:
\(f'(x)=3x^{2}+1\), so \(f'(1)=3+1=4\neq 0\).
\(\therefore\ \left(f^{-1}\right)'(0)=\frac{1}{f'(1)}=\frac{1}{4}\).

Let \(f(x)=\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x\), which is defined for every real \(x\).
Differentiating with respect to \(x\),
\(f'(x)=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}+\left(\frac{-1}{1+x^{2}}\right)=0\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).
A function whose derivative is zero throughout an interval is constant on that interval. Since \(\mathbb{R}\) is an interval,
\(f(x)=c\) for all \(x\), for some constant \(c\).
To find \(c\), put \(x=1\):
\(c=f(1)=\tan^{-1}1+\cot^{-1}1=\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
\(\therefore\ \tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}\) for every real \(x\).

Let \(f(x)=\sec^{-1}x+\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x\), which is defined for \(|x|\geq 1\).
For \(|x|>1\), differentiating with respect to \(x\),
\(f'(x)=\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}+\left(\frac{-1}{|x|\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}\right)=0\).
So \(f\) is constant on each of the intervals \((1,\infty)\) and \((-\infty,-1)\). Note that the domain is not a single interval, so the constant must be identified separately on each piece.
On \((1,\infty)\), put \(x=2\):
\(f(2)=\sec^{-1}2+\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}2=\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
On \((-\infty,-1)\), put \(x=-2\):
\(f(-2)=\sec^{-1}(-2)+\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-2)=\frac{2\pi}{3}+\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
Finally, at the two end points, \(f(1)=0+\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(f(-1)=\pi+\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
\(\therefore\ \sec^{-1}x+\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}\) for all \(|x|\geq 1\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}(\log x)\), \(x>0\).
Using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tan^{-1}u\right)=\frac{1}{1+u^{2}}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\) with \(u=\log x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+(\log x)^{2}}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(\log x)=\frac{1}{1+(\log x)^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{x}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{x\left[1+(\log x)^{2}\right]}\), for \(x>0\).

Let \(y=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(e^{-x}\right)\).
Domain: \(\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}u\) needs \(|u|\geq 1\), i.e. \(e^{-x}\geq 1\), i.e. \(x\leq 0\).
Using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}u\right)=\frac{-1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\) with \(u=e^{-x}\) (so \(|u|=e^{-x}\) and \(\frac{du}{dx}=-e^{-x}\)),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-1}{e^{-x}\sqrt{e^{-2x}-1}}\cdot\left(-e^{-x}\right)\).
The factors \(e^{-x}\) cancel, leaving
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{e^{-2x}-1}}\), for \(x<0\).

Let \(y=\cot^{-1}\left(x^{3}\right)\).
Using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\cot^{-1}u\right)=\frac{-1}{1+u^{2}}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\) with \(u=x^{3}\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-1}{1+\left(x^{3}\right)^{2}}\cdot 3x^{2}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-3x^{2}}{1+x^{6}}\).

Let \(y=\cot^{-1}\left(4^{x}\right)\).
Using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\cot^{-1}u\right)=\frac{-1}{1+u^{2}}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\) with \(u=4^{x}\), and \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(4^{x}\right)=4^{x}\log 4\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-1}{1+\left(4^{x}\right)^{2}}\cdot 4^{x}\log 4\).
Since \(\left(4^{x}\right)^{2}=4^{2x}=16^{x}\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-4^{x}\log 4}{1+16^{x}}\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)\), \(x>0\).
Using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tan^{-1}u\right)=\frac{1}{1+u^{2}}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\) with \(u=\sqrt{x}\), so that \(u^{2}=x\) and \(\frac{du}{dx}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+x}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}\,(1+x)}\), for \(x>0\).

Let \(y=\sin^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+x^{2}}{2}}\right)\).
Domain: we need \(\frac{1+x^{2}}{2}\leq 1\), i.e. \(x^{2}\leq 1\), i.e. \(|x|\leq 1\).
Put \(u=\sqrt{\frac{1+x^{2}}{2}}\), so \(u^{2}=\frac{1+x^{2}}{2}\).
Differentiating \(u^{2}=\frac{1+x^{2}}{2}\) with respect to \(x\) gives \(2u\frac{du}{dx}=x\), so \(\frac{du}{dx}=\frac{x}{2u}\).
Also \(1-u^{2}=1-\frac{1+x^{2}}{2}=\frac{1-x^{2}}{2}\), so \(\sqrt{1-u^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1-x^{2}}{2}}\).
Now
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}=\frac{x}{2u\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\).
The denominator simplifies: \(2u\sqrt{1-u^{2}}=2\sqrt{\frac{1+x^{2}}{2}\cdot\frac{1-x^{2}}{2}}=2\sqrt{\frac{1-x^{4}}{4}}=\sqrt{1-x^{4}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^{4}}}\), for \(0<|x|<1\).

Let \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(1-x^{2}\right)\).
Domain: \(-1\leq 1-x^{2}\leq 1\) gives \(0\leq x^{2}\leq 2\), i.e. \(|x|\leq\sqrt{2}\).
Using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\cos^{-1}u\right)=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\) with \(u=1-x^{2}\), \(\frac{du}{dx}=-2x\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{2}}}\cdot(-2x)=\frac{2x}{\sqrt{1-\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{2}}}\).
Now factorise the radicand as a difference of squares:
\(1-\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{2}=\left[1-\left(1-x^{2}\right)\right]\left[1+\left(1-x^{2}\right)\right]=x^{2}\left(2-x^{2}\right)\),
so \(\sqrt{1-\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{2}}=|x|\sqrt{2-x^{2}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2x}{|x|\sqrt{2-x^{2}}}\), for \(0<|x|<\sqrt{2}\).
The modulus makes the answer branch-dependent: \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2-x^{2}}}\) for \(x>0\), and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2}{\sqrt{2-x^{2}}}\) for \(x<0\).

Let \(y=\sin^{-1}\left(x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\).
Domain: \(x\geq 0\) (for \(x^{\frac{3}{2}}\) to be real) and \(x^{\frac{3}{2}}\leq 1\), so \(0\leq x\leq 1\).
Using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^{-1}u\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\) with \(u=x^{\frac{3}{2}}\), so \(u^{2}=x^{3}\) and \(\frac{du}{dx}=\frac{3}{2}x^{\frac{1}{2}}\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{3}}}\cdot\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{1-x^{3}}}\), for \(0<x<1\).

Let \(y=\cos^{3}\left[\cos^{-1}\left(x^{3}\right)\right]\).
Do not use the chain rule blindly here; first simplify using \(\cos\left(\cos^{-1}t\right)=t\), which is valid for \(|t|\leq 1\).
With \(t=x^{3}\) and \(|x|\leq 1\),
\(\cos\left[\cos^{-1}\left(x^{3}\right)\right]=x^{3}\).
Hence
\(y=\left(x^{3}\right)^{3}=x^{9}\), a simple power function.
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=9x^{8}\), for \(|x|\leq 1\).

Let \(y=\sin^{4}\left[\sin^{-1}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)\right]\).
First simplify using \(\sin\left(\sin^{-1}t\right)=t\), which is valid for \(|t|\leq 1\).
With \(t=\sqrt{x}\) and \(0\leq x\leq 1\),
\(\sin\left[\sin^{-1}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)\right]=\sqrt{x}\).
Hence
\(y=\left(\sqrt{x}\right)^{4}=x^{2}\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=2x\), for \(0\leq x\leq 1\).

Let \(y=\cot^{-1}\left[\cot\left(e^{x^{2}}\right)\right]\).
Use \(\cot^{-1}(\cot\theta)=\theta\), which holds only when \(\theta\) lies in the principal range \((0,\pi)\).
Here \(\theta=e^{x^{2}}\), and \(e^{x^{2}}>0\) always, so take \(x\) such that \(e^{x^{2}}<\pi\), i.e. \(x^{2}<\log\pi\). Then
\(y=e^{x^{2}}\).
Differentiating by the chain rule,
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x^{2}}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{2}\right)=e^{x^{2}}\cdot 2x\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=2x\,e^{x^{2}}\).

Let \(y=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\cos\left(5^{x}\right)}\right)=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(\sec\left(5^{x}\right)\right)\).
The key step is to convert the secant into a cosecant using the complementary-angle identity
\(\sec\theta=\operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\).
So, with \(\theta=5^{x}\),
\(y=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left[\operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-5^{x}\right)\right]\).
Now \(\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(\operatorname{cosec}\phi)=\phi\) for \(\phi\) in the principal range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(\phi\neq 0\). Taking \(5^{x}\) in \((0,\pi)\), \(5^{x}\neq\frac{\pi}{2}\), we get \(\phi=\frac{\pi}{2}-5^{x}\) in that range, so
\(y=\frac{\pi}{2}-5^{x}\).
Differentiating, and using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(5^{x}\right)=5^{x}\log 5\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-5^{x}\log 5\).

Let \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos x}{2}}\right)\).
Use the half-angle identity \(1+\cos x=2\cos^{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\), so
\(\frac{1+\cos x}{2}=\cos^{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\) and \(\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos x}{2}}=\left|\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\right|\).
Take \(x\in(0,\pi)\). Then \(\frac{x}{2}\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), so \(\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)>0\) and the modulus can be dropped:
\(y=\cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\right]=\frac{x}{2}\), since \(\frac{x}{2}\) lies in the principal range \([0,\pi]\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2}\), for \(x\in(0,\pi)\).
Note the branch matters: for \(x\in(\pi,2\pi)\) we would get \(y=\pi-\frac{x}{2}\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{2}\).

Let \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\left(x^{2}\right)}{2}}\right)\).
Use the half-angle identity \(1-\cos\theta=2\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\) with \(\theta=x^{2}\), so
\(\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\left(x^{2}\right)}{2}}=\left|\sin\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)\right|\).
Take \(x\) with \(0<x^{2}<\pi\). Then \(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), so \(\sin\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)>0\) and the modulus can be dropped:
\(y=\cos^{-1}\left[\sin\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)\right]\).
Now convert the sine into a cosine: \(\sin\phi=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\phi\right)\), and \(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x^{2}}{2}\) lies in \([0,\pi]\), so
\(y=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x^{2}}{2}\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-x\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1-\tan\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}{1+\tan\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}\right)\).
Since \(\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1\), the argument is exactly the expansion of \(\tan(A-B)\) with \(A=\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(B=\frac{x}{2}\):
\(\frac{1-\tan\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}{1+\tan\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}=\frac{\tan\frac{\pi}{4}-\tan\frac{x}{2}}{1+\tan\frac{\pi}{4}\tan\frac{x}{2}}=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{x}{2}\right)\).
Hence, taking \(x\) so that \(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{x}{2}\) lies in the principal range \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\),
\(y=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{x}{2}\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{2}\).

Let \(y=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{4\cos^{3}2x-3\cos 2x}\right)\).
Recognise the triple-angle identity \(\cos 3\theta=4\cos^{3}\theta-3\cos\theta\). With \(\theta=2x\),
\(4\cos^{3}2x-3\cos 2x=\cos 6x\).
So the argument is \(\frac{1}{\cos 6x}=\sec 6x\), and
\(y=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(\sec 6x)\).
Now use \(\sec\theta=\operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)\):
\(y=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left[\operatorname{cosec}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-6x\right)\right]=\frac{\pi}{2}-6x\),
taking \(6x\) in \((0,\pi)\), \(6x\neq\frac{\pi}{2}\), so that \(\frac{\pi}{2}-6x\) lies in the principal range.
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-6\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1+\cos\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)}\right)\).
Put \(\theta=\frac{x}{3}\) and use the half-angle identities \(1+\cos\theta=2\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\) and \(\sin\theta=2\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\):
\(\frac{1+\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\frac{2\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}{2\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}=\cot\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)=\cot\left(\frac{x}{6}\right)\).
Convert the cotangent into a tangent: \(\cot\phi=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\phi\right)\), so the argument is \(\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{6}\right)\).
Taking \(\frac{x}{6}\in(0,\pi)\), so that \(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{6}\) lies in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\),
\(y=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{6}\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{6}\).

Let \(y=\cot^{-1}\left(\frac{\sin 3x}{1+\cos 3x}\right)\).
Use the half-angle identities \(\sin 3x=2\sin\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)\) and \(1+\cos 3x=2\cos^{2}\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)\):
\(\frac{\sin 3x}{1+\cos 3x}=\frac{2\sin\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)}{2\cos^{2}\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)}=\tan\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right)\).
Convert the tangent into a cotangent: \(\tan\phi=\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\phi\right)\), so
\(y=\cot^{-1}\left[\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{3x}{2}\right)\right]=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{3x}{2}\),
taking \(x\) so that \(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{3x}{2}\) lies in the principal range \((0,\pi)\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{3}{2}\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\cos 7x}{1+\sin 7x}\right)\).
Put \(\theta=7x\) and write both parts in terms of \(\frac{\theta}{2}\):
\(\cos\theta=\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)-\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)=\left[\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)-\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right]\left[\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)+\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right]\),
\(1+\sin\theta=\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)+\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)+2\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)=\left[\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)+\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right]^{2}\).
Cancelling the common factor,
\(\frac{\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta}=\frac{\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)-\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)+\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}=\frac{1-\tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}{1+\tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\),
where the last step divides numerator and denominator by \(\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\) and uses \(\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1\).
Hence, taking \(x\) so that \(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{7x}{2}\) lies in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\),
\(y=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{7x}{2}\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{7}{2}\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos x}{1-\cos x}}\right)\).
Use the half-angle identities \(1+\cos x=2\cos^{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\) and \(1-\cos x=2\sin^{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\):
\(\frac{1+\cos x}{1-\cos x}=\frac{2\cos^{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}{2\sin^{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}=\cot^{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\), so \(\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos x}{1-\cos x}}=\left|\cot\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\right|\).
Take \(x\in(0,\pi)\). Then \(\frac{x}{2}\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), so \(\cot\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)>0\) and the modulus can be dropped:
\(y=\tan^{-1}\left[\cot\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\right]=\tan^{-1}\left[\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{2}\right)\right]=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{2}\),
since \(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{2}\) lies in \(\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{2}\), for \(x\in(0,\pi)\).
Note the branch matters: for \(x\in(\pi,2\pi)\) the modulus gives \(y=\frac{x}{2}-\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2}\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\operatorname{cosec}x+\cot x\right)\).
Combine the two terms over the common denominator \(\sin x\), then use the half-angle identities:
\(\operatorname{cosec}x+\cot x=\frac{1}{\sin x}+\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\frac{1+\cos x}{\sin x}=\frac{2\cos^{2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}{2\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}=\cot\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\).
Convert the cotangent into a tangent: \(\cot\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{2}\right)\).
Taking \(x\in(0,2\pi)\), \(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{2}\) lies in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), so
\(y=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{2}\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{2}\).

Let \(y=\cot^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{1+\sin\left(\frac{4x}{3}\right)}+\sqrt{1-\sin\left(\frac{4x}{3}\right)}}{\sqrt{1+\sin\left(\frac{4x}{3}\right)}-\sqrt{1-\sin\left(\frac{4x}{3}\right)}}\right)\).
Put \(\theta=\frac{4x}{3}\). The whole question turns on writing \(1\pm\sin\theta\) as a perfect square:
\(1\pm\sin\theta=\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)+\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\pm 2\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)=\left[\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\pm\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right]^{2}\).
Hence \(\sqrt{1\pm\sin\theta}=\left|\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\pm\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right|\).
Take \(\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{2x}{3}\) in \(\left(0,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\), i.e. \(0<x<\frac{3\pi}{8}\). Then \(\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)>\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)>0\), so both moduli open positively:
\(\sqrt{1+\sin\theta}=\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)+\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\) and \(\sqrt{1-\sin\theta}=\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)-\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\).
The numerator becomes \(2\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\) and the denominator \(2\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\), so the argument is
\(\frac{2\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}{2\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}=\cot\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)=\cot\left(\frac{2x}{3}\right)\).
Since \(\frac{2x}{3}\) lies in the principal range \((0,\pi)\),
\(y=\cot^{-1}\left[\cot\left(\frac{2x}{3}\right)\right]=\frac{2x}{3}\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{3}\).

Let \(y=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{4\sin x+5\cos x}{\sqrt{41}}\right)\).
Notice \(4^{2}+5^{2}=41\), which is the clue: introduce a constant angle \(\alpha\) with
\(\cos\alpha=\frac{4}{\sqrt{41}}\), \(\sin\alpha=\frac{5}{\sqrt{41}}\), i.e. \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)\).
Then
\(\frac{4\sin x+5\cos x}{\sqrt{41}}=\sin x\cos\alpha+\cos x\sin\alpha=\sin(x+\alpha)\).
Hence, taking \(x+\alpha\) in the principal range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\),
\(y=\sin^{-1}\left[\sin(x+\alpha)\right]=x+\alpha=x+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)\).
Since \(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)\) is a constant, its derivative is zero.
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=1\).

Let \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}\cos x-\sin x}{2}\right)\).
Split the coefficients as cosine and sine of a standard angle: \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\cos\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{1}{2}=\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\). Then
\(\frac{\sqrt{3}\cos x-\sin x}{2}=\cos x\cos\frac{\pi}{6}-\sin x\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\).
Hence, taking \(x+\frac{\pi}{6}\) in the principal range \([0,\pi]\),
\(y=\cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]=x+\frac{\pi}{6}\).
Differentiating (the \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) is a constant),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=1\).

Let \(y=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\cos\sqrt{x}+\sin\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\), \(x>0\).
Since \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\), rewrite the argument as
\(\sin\sqrt{x}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\cos\sqrt{x}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\sin\sqrt{x}\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+\cos\sqrt{x}\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=\sin\left(\sqrt{x}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\).
Hence, taking \(\sqrt{x}+\frac{\pi}{4}\) in the principal range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) (i.e. \(0\leq\sqrt{x}\leq\frac{\pi}{4}\)),
\(y=\sqrt{x}+\frac{\pi}{4}\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\), for \(x>0\).

Let \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{3\cos 3x-4\sin 3x}{5}\right)\).
Notice \(3^{2}+4^{2}=25\): introduce a constant angle \(\alpha\) with
\(\cos\alpha=\frac{3}{5}\), \(\sin\alpha=\frac{4}{5}\), i.e. \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\).
Then
\(\frac{3\cos 3x-4\sin 3x}{5}=\cos 3x\cos\alpha-\sin 3x\sin\alpha=\cos(3x+\alpha)\).
Hence, taking \(3x+\alpha\) in the principal range \([0,\pi]\),
\(y=\cos^{-1}\left[\cos(3x+\alpha)\right]=3x+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\).
Differentiating (the inverse-tangent term is a constant),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=3\).

Let \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{3\cos\left(e^{x}\right)+2\sin\left(e^{x}\right)}{\sqrt{13}}\right)\).
Notice \(3^{2}+2^{2}=13\): introduce a constant angle \(\alpha\) with
\(\cos\alpha=\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\), \(\sin\alpha=\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\), i.e. \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\).
Writing \(u=e^{x}\),
\(\frac{3\cos u+2\sin u}{\sqrt{13}}=\cos u\cos\alpha+\sin u\sin\alpha=\cos(u-\alpha)\).
Hence, taking \(u-\alpha\) in the principal range \([0,\pi]\),
\(y=\cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(e^{x}-\alpha\right)\right]=e^{x}-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\).
Differentiating (the inverse-tangent term is a constant),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x}\).

Let \(y=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(\frac{10}{6\sin\left(2^{x}\right)-8\cos\left(2^{x}\right)}\right)\).
Notice \(6^{2}+8^{2}=100=10^{2}\): introduce a constant angle \(\alpha\) with
\(\cos\alpha=\frac{6}{10}=\frac{3}{5}\), \(\sin\alpha=\frac{8}{10}=\frac{4}{5}\), i.e. \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\).
Writing \(u=2^{x}\),
\(6\sin u-8\cos u=10\left(\sin u\cos\alpha-\cos u\sin\alpha\right)=10\sin(u-\alpha)\).
So the argument becomes
\(\frac{10}{10\sin(u-\alpha)}=\frac{1}{\sin(u-\alpha)}=\operatorname{cosec}(u-\alpha)\).
Hence, taking \(u-\alpha\) in the principal range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(u-\alpha\neq 0\),
\(y=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left[\operatorname{cosec}\left(2^{x}-\alpha\right)\right]=2^{x}-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\).
Differentiating, and using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(2^{x}\right)=2^{x}\log 2\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=2^{x}\log 2\).

Let \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}\right)\).
Put \(x=\tan\theta\), so that \(\theta=\tan^{-1}x\) lies in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Then
\(\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}=\frac{1-\tan^{2}\theta}{1+\tan^{2}\theta}=\cos 2\theta\),
so \(y=\cos^{-1}(\cos 2\theta)\). Now the principal branch decides the sign, and the two cases genuinely differ.
Case \(x>0\): then \(\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), so \(2\theta\in(0,\pi)\), which IS the principal range of \(\cos^{-1}\). Hence
\(y=2\theta=2\tan^{-1}x\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{1+x^{2}}\).
Case \(x<0\): then \(2\theta\in(-\pi,0)\), outside the principal range. Using \(\cos 2\theta=\cos(-2\theta)\) with \(-2\theta\in(0,\pi)\),
\(y=-2\theta=-2\tan^{-1}x\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2}{1+x^{2}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{1+x^{2}}\) for \(x>0\), and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2}{1+x^{2}}\) for \(x<0\). (At \(x=0\) the function is not differentiable.)

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2x}{1-x^{2}}\right)\).
Put \(x=\tan\theta\), so \(\theta=\tan^{-1}x\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Then
\(\frac{2x}{1-x^{2}}=\frac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^{2}\theta}=\tan 2\theta\).
For \(|x|<1\) we have \(\theta\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\), so \(2\theta\) lies in the principal range \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and
\(y=2\theta=2\tan^{-1}x\).
Differentiating,
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{1+x^{2}}\).
For \(|x|>1\) the value of \(y\) differs from \(2\tan^{-1}x\) only by the constant \(\pi\) or \(-\pi\), and a constant has zero derivative, so the same expression holds.
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{1+x^{2}}\), for all \(x\neq\pm 1\).

Let \(y=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}\right)\). (Compare Q.9 (i): the argument is the same but the inverse function is \(\sin^{-1}\), and the answer differs in sign.)
Put \(x=\tan\theta\), so \(\theta=\tan^{-1}x\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Then
\(\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}=\cos 2\theta\).
To use \(\sin^{-1}\) we must convert the cosine into a sine: \(\cos 2\theta=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-2\theta\right)\).
Case \(x>0\): then \(\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), so \(\frac{\pi}{2}-2\theta\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), which IS the principal range of \(\sin^{-1}\). Hence
\(y=\frac{\pi}{2}-2\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}-2\tan^{-1}x\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2}{1+x^{2}}\).
Case \(x<0\): then \(\frac{\pi}{2}-2\theta\in\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)\), outside the principal range. Using \(\cos 2\theta=\cos(-2\theta)=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+2\theta\right)\), with \(\frac{\pi}{2}+2\theta\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\),
\(y=\frac{\pi}{2}+2\tan^{-1}x\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{1+x^{2}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2}{1+x^{2}}\) for \(x>0\), and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{1+x^{2}}\) for \(x<0\).

Let \(y=\sin^{-1}\left(2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)\).
Put \(x=\sin\theta\), so \(\theta=\sin^{-1}x\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\). On this range \(\cos\theta\geq 0\), so \(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=\cos\theta\) (no modulus needed). Then
\(2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin 2\theta\).
For \(|x|<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) we have \(\theta\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\), so \(2\theta\) lies in the principal range \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and
\(y=2\theta=2\sin^{-1}x\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\), for \(|x|<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).
The branch matters: for \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}<x<1\) one gets \(y=\pi-2\sin^{-1}x\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\).

Let \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(3x-4x^{3}\right)\).
Put \(x=\sin\theta\), so \(\theta=\sin^{-1}x\). Recognise the triple-angle identity \(\sin 3\theta=3\sin\theta-4\sin^{3}\theta\):
\(3x-4x^{3}=3\sin\theta-4\sin^{3}\theta=\sin 3\theta\).
So \(y=\cos^{-1}(\sin 3\theta)\). Convert the sine into a cosine using \(\sin\phi=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\phi\right)\):
\(y=\cos^{-1}\left[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-3\theta\right)\right]\).
Take \(|x|\leq\frac{1}{2}\), so \(\theta\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6}\right]\) and \(3\theta\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\); then \(\frac{\pi}{2}-3\theta\) lies in the principal range \([0,\pi]\) and
\(y=\frac{\pi}{2}-3\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}-3\sin^{-1}x\).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-3}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\), for \(|x|<\frac{1}{2}\).

Let \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{e^{x}+e^{-x}}\right)\).
Here no trigonometric substitution is needed; differentiate directly and let the algebra collapse.
Put \(u=\frac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{e^{x}+e^{-x}}\). By the quotient rule,
\(\frac{du}{dx}=\frac{\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)-\left(e^{x}-e^{-x}\right)\left(e^{x}-e^{-x}\right)}{\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)^{2}}=\frac{\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)^{2}-\left(e^{x}-e^{-x}\right)^{2}}{\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)^{2}}=\frac{4}{\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)^{2}}\),
using \((a+b)^{2}-(a-b)^{2}=4ab\) with \(ab=e^{x}\cdot e^{-x}=1\).
The same identity gives
\(1-u^{2}=\frac{\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)^{2}-\left(e^{x}-e^{-x}\right)^{2}}{\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)^{2}}=\frac{4}{\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)^{2}}\), so \(\sqrt{1-u^{2}}=\frac{2}{e^{x}+e^{-x}}\).
Hence
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}=-\frac{e^{x}+e^{-x}}{2}\cdot\frac{4}{\left(e^{x}+e^{-x}\right)^{2}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2}{e^{x}+e^{-x}}\).

Let \(y=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-9^{x}}{1+9^{x}}\right)\).
The clue is \(9^{x}=\left(3^{x}\right)^{2}\), so the argument has the shape \(\frac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}\) with \(t=3^{x}\).
Put \(3^{x}=\tan\theta\), i.e. \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(3^{x}\right)\). Since \(3^{x}>0\) for every \(x\), \(\theta\) lies in \(\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Then
\(\frac{1-9^{x}}{1+9^{x}}=\frac{1-\tan^{2}\theta}{1+\tan^{2}\theta}=\cos 2\theta\).
Because \(\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), \(2\theta\in(0,\pi)\), which IS the principal range of \(\cos^{-1}\). So, unlike Q.9 (i), there is no second case here.
\(y=2\theta=2\tan^{-1}\left(3^{x}\right)\).
Differentiating, and using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(3^{x}\right)=3^{x}\log 3\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=2\cdot\frac{1}{1+\left(3^{x}\right)^{2}}\cdot 3^{x}\log 3\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\cdot 3^{x}\log 3}{1+9^{x}}\).

Let \(y=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{4^{x+\frac{1}{2}}}{1+2^{4x}}\right)\).
First tidy the powers. The half-integer exponent is the point of the question:
\(4^{x+\frac{1}{2}}=4^{x}\cdot 4^{\frac{1}{2}}=2\cdot 4^{x}\), and \(2^{4x}=\left(2^{2x}\right)^{2}=\left(4^{x}\right)^{2}\).
So, writing \(t=4^{x}\), the argument becomes \(\frac{2t}{1+t^{2}}\), the standard form.
Put \(t=\tan\theta\), i.e. \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(4^{x}\right)\); since \(4^{x}>0\), \(\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Then
\(\frac{2t}{1+t^{2}}=\frac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^{2}\theta}=\sin 2\theta\).
Case \(x<0\): then \(t=4^{x}<1\), so \(\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) and \(2\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), inside the principal range of \(\sin^{-1}\). Hence
\(y=2\theta=2\tan^{-1}\left(4^{x}\right)\), and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=2\cdot\frac{4^{x}\log 4}{1+\left(4^{x}\right)^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot 4^{x}\log 4}{1+16^{x}}\).
Case \(x>0\): then \(t>1\) and \(2\theta\in\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)\), outside the principal range; there \(y=\pi-2\tan^{-1}\left(4^{x}\right)\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2\cdot 4^{x}\log 4}{1+16^{x}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\cdot 4^{x}\log 4}{1+16^{x}}\) for \(x<0\), with the sign reversed for \(x>0\).

Let \(y=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1-25x^{2}}{1+25x^{2}}\right)\).
Since \(25x^{2}=(5x)^{2}\), the argument has the shape \(\frac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}\) with \(t=5x\).
Put \(5x=\tan\theta\), i.e. \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(5x)\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Then
\(\frac{1-25x^{2}}{1+25x^{2}}=\cos 2\theta=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-2\theta\right)\).
Case \(x>0\): then \(\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), so \(\frac{\pi}{2}-2\theta\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), the principal range. Hence
\(y=\frac{\pi}{2}-2\tan^{-1}(5x)\), and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=-2\cdot\frac{5}{1+25x^{2}}=\frac{-10}{1+25x^{2}}\).
Case \(x<0\): by the same argument as in Q.9 (iii), \(y=\frac{\pi}{2}+2\tan^{-1}(5x)\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{10}{1+25x^{2}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-10}{1+25x^{2}}\) for \(x>0\), and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{10}{1+25x^{2}}\) for \(x<0\).

Let \(y=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^{3}}{1+x^{3}}\right)\).
The argument has the shape \(\frac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}\) with \(t^{2}=x^{3}\), i.e. \(t=x^{\frac{3}{2}}\), which requires \(x\geq 0\).
Put \(x^{\frac{3}{2}}=\tan\theta\), i.e. \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Then
\(\frac{1-x^{3}}{1+x^{3}}=\frac{1-\tan^{2}\theta}{1+\tan^{2}\theta}=\cos 2\theta=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-2\theta\right)\).
Since \(\theta\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), we get \(\frac{\pi}{2}-2\theta\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), which lies in the principal range of \(\sin^{-1}\). Hence
\(y=\frac{\pi}{2}-2\tan^{-1}\left(x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\).
Differentiating, with \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=-2\cdot\frac{1}{1+x^{3}}\cdot\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-3\sqrt{x}}{1+x^{3}}\), for \(x>0\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{1-x^{5}}\right)\).
The argument has the shape \(\frac{2t}{1-t^{2}}\) with \(t=x^{\frac{5}{2}}\) (so \(t^{2}=x^{5}\)); this needs \(x\geq 0\).
Put \(x^{\frac{5}{2}}=\tan\theta\), i.e. \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(x^{\frac{5}{2}}\right)\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Then
\(\frac{2x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{1-x^{5}}=\frac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^{2}\theta}=\tan 2\theta\).
For \(0\leq x<1\) we have \(\theta\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\), so \(2\theta\) lies in the principal range \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and
\(y=2\theta=2\tan^{-1}\left(x^{\frac{5}{2}}\right)\).
Differentiating, with \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{\frac{5}{2}}\right)=\frac{5}{2}x^{\frac{3}{2}}\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=2\cdot\frac{1}{1+x^{5}}\cdot\frac{5}{2}x^{\frac{3}{2}}=\frac{5x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{1+x^{5}}\).
For \(x>1\) the value of \(y\) differs only by the constant \(\pi\), so the derivative is unchanged.
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{5x\sqrt{x}}{1+x^{5}}\), for \(x>0\), \(x\neq 1\).

Let \(y=\cot^{-1}\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{1+\sqrt{x}}\right)\), \(x>0\).
Put \(\sqrt{x}=\tan\theta\), i.e. \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Since \(\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1\),
\(\frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{1+\sqrt{x}}=\frac{\tan\frac{\pi}{4}-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\frac{\pi}{4}\tan\theta}=\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\theta\right)\).
The outer function is \(\cot^{-1}\), so convert the tangent into a cotangent using \(\tan\phi=\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\phi\right)\):
\(\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\theta\right)=\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{4}+\theta\right)=\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{4}+\theta\right)\).
Since \(\theta\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), we get \(\frac{\pi}{4}+\theta\in\left[\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\), which lies in the principal range \((0,\pi)\) of \(\cot^{-1}\). Hence
\(y=\frac{\pi}{4}+\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}+\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)\).
Differentiating (the \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) is a constant),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+x}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}\,(1+x)}\), for \(x>0\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{8x}{1-15x^{2}}\right)\).
The technique is to split the argument into the form \(\frac{A+B}{1-AB}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}A+\tan^{-1}B\right)\).
Look for \(A\) and \(B\) with \(A+B=8x\) and \(AB=15x^{2}\): taking \(A=5x\) and \(B=3x\) works, since \(5x+3x=8x\) and \((5x)(3x)=15x^{2}\).
Hence
\(\frac{8x}{1-15x^{2}}=\frac{5x+3x}{1-(5x)(3x)}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}5x+\tan^{-1}3x\right)\),
so, on the appropriate branch,
\(y=\tan^{-1}5x+\tan^{-1}3x\).
(On other branches \(y\) differs only by the constant \(\pi\), which does not affect the derivative.)
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{5}{1+25x^{2}}+\frac{3}{1+9x^{2}}\).

Let \(y=\cot^{-1}\left(\frac{1+35x^{2}}{2x}\right)\).
Since the argument of \(\cot^{-1}\) is the reciprocal of a tangent, work with \(\frac{2x}{1+35x^{2}}\) and split it into the form \(\frac{A-B}{1+AB}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}A-\tan^{-1}B\right)\).
Look for \(A\) and \(B\) with \(A-B=2x\) and \(AB=35x^{2}\): taking \(A=7x\) and \(B=5x\) works, since \(7x-5x=2x\) and \((7x)(5x)=35x^{2}\).
Hence
\(\frac{2x}{1+35x^{2}}=\frac{7x-5x}{1+(7x)(5x)}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}7x-\tan^{-1}5x\right)\),
and therefore
\(\frac{1+35x^{2}}{2x}=\cot\left(\tan^{-1}7x-\tan^{-1}5x\right)\).
So, on the appropriate branch,
\(y=\tan^{-1}7x-\tan^{-1}5x\)
(on other branches \(y\) differs only by the constant \(\pi\), which does not affect the derivative).
Differentiating,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{7}{1+49x^{2}}-\frac{5}{1+25x^{2}}\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{1+3x}\right)\), \(x>0\).
The \(+\) sign in the denominator points to the difference form \(\frac{A-B}{1+AB}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}A-\tan^{-1}B\right)\).
Look for \(A\) and \(B\) with \(A-B=2\sqrt{x}\) and \(AB=3x\): taking \(A=3\sqrt{x}\) and \(B=\sqrt{x}\) works, since \(3\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{x}=2\sqrt{x}\) and \(\left(3\sqrt{x}\right)\left(\sqrt{x}\right)=3x\).
Hence
\(\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{1+3x}=\frac{3\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{x}}{1+\left(3\sqrt{x}\right)\left(\sqrt{x}\right)}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}\left(3\sqrt{x}\right)-\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)\right)\),
so
\(y=\tan^{-1}\left(3\sqrt{x}\right)-\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)\).
Differentiating each term by the chain rule, with \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+9x}\cdot\frac{3}{2\sqrt{x}}-\frac{1}{1+x}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{x}\,(1+9x)}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}\,(1+x)}\), for \(x>0\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2^{x+2}}{1-3\left(4^{x}\right)}\right)\).
First tidy the powers: \(2^{x+2}=4\cdot 2^{x}\) and \(4^{x}=\left(2^{x}\right)^{2}\). Writing \(t=2^{x}\), the argument is \(\frac{4t}{1-3t^{2}}\).
Split it into the form \(\frac{A+B}{1-AB}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}A+\tan^{-1}B\right)\): we need \(A+B=4t\) and \(AB=3t^{2}\), so take \(A=3t\) and \(B=t\), since \(3t+t=4t\) and \((3t)(t)=3t^{2}\).
Hence
\(\frac{4t}{1-3t^{2}}=\frac{3t+t}{1-(3t)(t)}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}3t+\tan^{-1}t\right)\),
so, on the appropriate branch,
\(y=\tan^{-1}\left(3\cdot 2^{x}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(2^{x}\right)\).
Differentiating, and using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(2^{x}\right)=2^{x}\log 2\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3\cdot 2^{x}\log 2}{1+\left(3\cdot 2^{x}\right)^{2}}+\frac{2^{x}\log 2}{1+\left(2^{x}\right)^{2}}\).
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3\cdot 2^{x}\log 2}{1+9\cdot 4^{x}}+\frac{2^{x}\log 2}{1+4^{x}}\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2^{x}}{1+2^{2x+1}}\right)\).
First tidy the powers: \(2^{2x+1}=2\cdot 2^{2x}=2\left(2^{x}\right)^{2}\). Writing \(t=2^{x}\), the argument is \(\frac{t}{1+2t^{2}}\).
The \(+\) sign in the denominator points to the difference form \(\frac{A-B}{1+AB}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}A-\tan^{-1}B\right)\): we need \(A-B=t\) and \(AB=2t^{2}\), so take \(A=2t\) and \(B=t\), since \(2t-t=t\) and \((2t)(t)=2t^{2}\).
Hence
\(\frac{t}{1+2t^{2}}=\frac{2t-t}{1+(2t)(t)}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}2t-\tan^{-1}t\right)\),
so, noting \(2t=2\cdot 2^{x}=2^{x+1}\),
\(y=\tan^{-1}\left(2^{x+1}\right)-\tan^{-1}\left(2^{x}\right)\).
Differentiating, and using \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(2^{x+1}\right)=2^{x+1}\log 2\) and \(\left(2^{x+1}\right)^{2}=4^{x+1}\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2^{x+1}\log 2}{1+4^{x+1}}-\frac{2^{x}\log 2}{1+4^{x}}\).

Let \(y=\cot^{-1}\left(\frac{a^{2}-6x^{2}}{5ax}\right)\).
Divide the numerator and the denominator by \(a^{2}\) to expose the standard shape:
\(\frac{a^{2}-6x^{2}}{5ax}=\frac{1-6\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^{2}}{5\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)}\).
Write \(t=\frac{x}{a}\). Since \(\cot^{-1}\) takes the reciprocal of a tangent, work with \(\frac{5t}{1-6t^{2}}\) and split it into \(\frac{A+B}{1-AB}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}A+\tan^{-1}B\right)\): we need \(A+B=5t\) and \(AB=6t^{2}\), so take \(A=3t\) and \(B=2t\).
Hence
\(\frac{5t}{1-6t^{2}}=\frac{3t+2t}{1-(3t)(2t)}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}3t+\tan^{-1}2t\right)\),
so the given argument is \(\cot\left(\tan^{-1}3t+\tan^{-1}2t\right)\), and on the appropriate branch
\(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3x}{a}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2x}{a}\right)\).
Differentiating (with \(a\) constant),
\(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{9x^{2}}{a^{2}}}\cdot\frac{3}{a}+\frac{1}{1+\frac{4x^{2}}{a^{2}}}\cdot\frac{2}{a}\).
Multiplying numerator and denominator of each term by \(a^{2}\),
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3a}{a^{2}+9x^{2}}+\frac{2a}{a^{2}+4x^{2}}\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{a+b\tan x}{b-a\tan x}\right)\).
Divide the numerator and the denominator by \(b\):
\(\frac{a+b\tan x}{b-a\tan x}=\frac{\frac{a}{b}+\tan x}{1-\frac{a}{b}\tan x}\).
This is exactly the expansion of \(\tan(A+B)=\frac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B}\) with \(\tan A=\frac{a}{b}\) and \(\tan B=\tan x\), i.e.
\(\frac{a+b\tan x}{b-a\tan x}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)+x\right)\).
Hence, on the appropriate branch,
\(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)+x\).
Now \(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)\) is a constant (it involves no \(x\)), so its derivative is zero.
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=1\).

Let \(y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5-x}{6x^{2}-5x-3}\right)\).
The denominator does not factorise over the rationals (its discriminant is \(25+72=97\)), so do not try to factorise it. Instead split the whole fraction into the form \(\frac{A-B}{1+AB}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}A-\tan^{-1}B\right)\).
Try \(A=2x+1\) and \(B=3x-4\). Then
\(A-B=(2x+1)-(3x-4)=5-x\), which matches the numerator, and
\(1+AB=1+(2x+1)(3x-4)=1+\left(6x^{2}-8x+3x-4\right)=6x^{2}-5x-3\), which matches the denominator.
Hence
\(\frac{5-x}{6x^{2}-5x-3}=\frac{(2x+1)-(3x-4)}{1+(2x+1)(3x-4)}=\tan\left[\tan^{-1}(2x+1)-\tan^{-1}(3x-4)\right]\),
so, on the appropriate branch,
\(y=\tan^{-1}(2x+1)-\tan^{-1}(3x-4)\).
Differentiating each term by the chain rule,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{1+(2x+1)^{2}}-\frac{3}{1+(3x-4)^{2}}\).

Let \(y=\cot^{-1}\left(\frac{4-x-2x^{2}}{3x+2}\right)\).
Since \(\cot^{-1}\) takes the reciprocal of a tangent, work with \(\frac{3x+2}{4-x-2x^{2}}\) and split it into the form \(\frac{A+B}{1-AB}=\tan\left(\tan^{-1}A+\tan^{-1}B\right)\).
Try \(A=x-1\) and \(B=2x+3\). Then
\(A+B=(x-1)+(2x+3)=3x+2\), which matches the numerator, and
\(1-AB=1-(x-1)(2x+3)=1-\left(2x^{2}+x-3\right)=4-x-2x^{2}\), which matches the denominator.
Hence
\(\frac{3x+2}{4-x-2x^{2}}=\tan\left[\tan^{-1}(x-1)+\tan^{-1}(2x+3)\right]\),
and therefore the given argument is
\(\frac{4-x-2x^{2}}{3x+2}=\cot\left[\tan^{-1}(x-1)+\tan^{-1}(2x+3)\right]\).
So, on the appropriate branch,
\(y=\tan^{-1}(x-1)+\tan^{-1}(2x+3)\).
Differentiating each term by the chain rule,
\(\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+(x-1)^{2}}+\frac{2}{1+(2x+3)^{2}}\).
